title: Arjuna asks, why act at all?
hook: Arjuna catches his teacher in what looks like a contradiction
carry: karma yoga: work offered to god doesn't bind

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Tagore's Gitanjali with a prayer for a mind without fear: abhaya, the raised palm that says fear not.

If understanding is better than action, why push me into this terrible deed? That, in paraphrase, is how chapter three of the Gita begins. In chapter two, Krishna praised a steady understanding and said plain action falls far below it. And all along, he'd been telling Arjuna to stand up and fight. Arjuna is confused, and a little irritated. Your words seem mixed, he says. Tell me the one thing that's good for me. Now we read these chapters again, slowly, with the old commentators at our elbow.
screen: `WHY PUSH ME INTO THIS DEED?` → `YOUR WORDS SEEM MIXED.` → `READ AGAIN, WITH COMMENTARY.`

segments.voice: Nobody can stay even a moment without acting. Every being is made to act by the forces of its own nature. Sitting still is an act. Breathing is an act. So the question was never whether to act, but how. Here Krishna brings in an old word: yajna, sacrifice, offering. The world is bound by action, he says, except action done as offering. Do your work in that spirit, free of clinging. Then a short creation story. In the beginning, the Creator brought forth beings together with sacrifice and said: by this you will flourish. You nourish the gods, and the gods will nourish you. Rain, food, work, offering, rain again. Krishna calls it a wheel set turning, and says a person who takes from it and doesn't help turn it lives in vain. So karma, in chapter three, is first the plain word for action, and only then the web of consequences it sets going. This is karma yoga, the yoga of action: you can't stop working, so offer the work, and it stops binding you. It's why many Hindus offer food to God before they eat, or quietly offer a day's work before they begin it. Shankara, glossing sacrifice in this verse, says it means the Lord himself, and quotes an older Vedic line: sacrifice is Vishnu. So for him, action done as offering is action done for God. Either way, the verse says the same thing about the doer: act, and let go of the grip.
screen: `NOBODY STAYS A MOMENT WITHOUT ACTING.` · `THE QUESTION IS WHAT KIND OF ACTION.` · `ACTION DONE AS OFFERING DOESN'T BIND.` · `THE WHEEL: NOURISH AND BE NOURISHED.` · then, large: `KARMA YOGA: OFFER THE WORK.`

segments.voice: For the first few breaths, try to do nothing at all, and notice that you can't: the breath goes on, the heart goes on, the body keeps its balance. Then find one place in an ordinary day where you mostly take from the wheel and give little back, without judging it, and one small way to put something back. If you pray, you can hold that small return before Krishna, or the one you pray to.
Karma. In chapter three, first the plain word for action, which nobody escapes; done as an offering, it becomes karma yoga, and doesn't bind.
Your line: karma yoga: work offered to God doesn't bind. Tomorrow, a king who was also a sage. See you then.

howItsDone: Some Hindus begin a day's work, or a meal, by mentally offering it to God, and some Gita study groups read chapter three alongside a classical commentary such as Shankara's.

yajna.meaning: sacrifice, offering: action given back, like rain feeding the wheel

Shankara.meaning: a great teacher of non-duality who wrote a Gita commentary

Vedic.meaning: from the Vedas, the oldest Hindu scriptures

Vishnu.meaning: the God who preserves the world; many see Krishna as his avatar

karma yoga.meaning: the yoga of action: work done as an offering, without clinging to the fruit
